Q: How to increase the resolution of ggplots in Rmarkdown html files A:

I had the same problem and what saved me was this part of the R-markdown cookbook (Chapter 11.15):

"Usually, vector graphics have higher quality than raster graphics, and you can scale vector graphics without loss of quality. For HTML output, you may consider using dev = "svg" or dev = "svglite" for SVG plots. Note that SVG is a vector graphics format, and the default png device produces a raster graphics format." [1]

Before this, I also tried many combinations of increasing and changing the dpi, fig.width, fig.height or fig.retina and I never managed to get a good looking output in a short amount of time. However, when you have a ggplot you can add dev="svg" to your chunk options and your figures will look sharper. As a small bonus, the file size of the output HTML appears to be a little bit smaller when using dev = "svg" for your plots.

Here is an example:


library(ggplot2)
test_data <- head(iris)
test_plot <- ggplot(test_data) + 
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width),
             size = 7)

SVG

```{r plot-svg, dev = "svg"}
test_plot


### PNG

```markdown
```{r plot-png, dev = "png"}
test_plot


### PNG + higher dpi

When knitting to Word, increasing the dpi results in high resolution images of the same size. When knitting to HTML the overall plot size increases.

```markdown
```{r plot-png-dpi, dev = "png", dpi = 300}
test_plot


A small disclaimer: When you already have figured out the appropriate `fig.width` and `fig.height` of your plot and change the device to "svg", those options might need to be changed again.

\[1\] Yihui Xie, Christophe Dervieux, Emily Riederer, R Markdown Cookbook 

https://yihui.org/rmarkdown-cookbook/

Q: Can't figure out the real way to learn the C++ language? A:

You have to free yourself of some misunderstandings.

  • Courses at university about software fundamentals have one aim: to teach you software fundamentals not C++. The language is merely used as a vehicle.
  • C++ is not C. C++ is also not just a superset of C. They are two different languages. There is no language called C/C++.
  • Just because you can write low level code, does not mean you have to or should.
  • Nobody knows all C++.
  • The standard is not written to learn the language. Scott Meyers books were written for that (well there are also others)
  • Standard libraries are not good examples of C++ code. Implementations can exploit implementation details that you better be agnostic about.

There is an excellent talk about first points that I can only recommend to watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YnWhqhNdYyk

Starting from scratch is a good attitude because it makes space for relearning. Don't get overwhelmed by the size of the language. It is huge and it gets bigger with every standard version. C++ was never famous for being easy to teach or learn. And don't rush.

Q: How to publish a Google form with Google Scripts? A:

From the question

The problem is that recently Google is requiring to publish forms before using them. I tried to look for some function to use it in GAS but I do not find any. Can anyone tell me a way to publish forms in a script, so I do not have to do it manually?

You are referring to the change announced in Adding granular control options for who can respond to Google Forms.

This announcement does not mention an update or change to the Google Apps Script, and the Google Apps Script release notes do not say anything new related to Google Forms.

Remarks

  • Only new forms are required to be published.
  • There is no mention of how this change affects the new forms created using the Apps Script Forms Service

Considering the above, I suggest you try to create a new form using the Forms Service and check if they are required to be published or not.

Test code

The following code creates a new Google Form using the Forms Service, then prints the published form URL to the execution logs.

function myFunction() {
  const form = FormApp.create("Test");
  const url = form.getPublishedUrl();
  Logger.log(url);
}

When opening the form in the Google Forms editor, it shows that it is already published.
